result:
There is a peculiar hour just before dawn when the world seems undecided.

Streetlights still burn, though their work is nearly done. Birds test a few uncertain notes. Windows remain dark, holding the dreams of strangers. Even time appears to pause at the threshold, one hand resting on night and the other reaching toward morning.

I like to imagine that unfinished things gather there: apologies never spoken, letters abandoned after “Dear,” plans postponed until a braver season. For a few minutes, none of them have failed. They are simply waiting.

Then the sky begins to lighten—not dramatically, but by degrees too small to witness. Black becomes blue. Shapes recover their names. A roof, a tree, a road. The ordinary world returns piece by piece.

Perhaps change usually happens this way. Not as thunder, not as revelation, but as a slow accumulation of almost nothing: one honest sentence, one glass of water, one walk around the block, one more attempt.

And then, somehow, it is morning.
